summaries: Requester: Mr. Stephen Bright. Question: Are the custodian's decisions to classify the requested records as personnel records and employee-evaluation records and to release those records with redactions consistent with the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)? Brief Response: In my opinion, the custodian's decisions are partially consistent with the FOIA. The custodian has correctly classified the first three groups of records as personnel records and has properly determined that they are subject to release, with the employee's personnel number redacted. With respect to the fourth set of records, I cannot definitively say whether every record in that set has been properly classified as an employee-evaluation record because the copies provided to this Office contain extensive redactions. I can say, however, that at least the first portion of that set—the Notice of Disciplinary Action—qualifies as an evaluation record. The custodian's determination that the employee-evaluation records are releasable is also consistent with the FOIA because the employee was suspended, his suspension is final, the records relate to that suspension, and there is a compelling public interest in their disclosure. The custodian has, however, made extensive redactions to the records that she has classified as employee-evaluation records. As a general matter, when an employee-evaluation record is subject to disclosure, it should be released in its entirety, and redactions should be made only if a separate exemption applies. If the custodian's redactions to the evaluation records are based on A.C.A. § 25-19-105(b)(12)'s balancing test, those redactions are improper. I cannot definitively reach that conclusion, however, because the custodian has not provided this Office with unredacted copies of the records and has not identified the basis for the redactions. Under A.C.A. § 25-19-105(a)(3)(B), if responsive records are subject to exemptions, the custodian must identify the applicable exemptions.

Requester: State Senator Scott Flippo. Question 1: Were Hospice of the Ozarks, Inc.'s Articles of Incorporation violated or disregarded? Question 2: Was the board of Hospice of the Ozarks, Inc. lawfully constituted at the time the bylaws were amended? Question 3: Were fiduciary duties owed to Hospice of the Ozarks, Inc. and its charitable purpose upheld? Question 4: Is any corrective or enforcement action warranted under Arkansas law? Brief Response: Unfortunately, I am unable to respond to your specific questions because they require factual determinations regarding the actions of private nonprofit corporations, the appointments of directors, the amendment of bylaws, and whether particular individuals complied with fiduciary duties. This Office has consistently declined to resolve questions of fact in the context of an Attorney General opinion. Additionally, your questions concern the rights, duties, and actions of private parties under specific corporate governing documents. This Office is not positioned to interpret the specific terms of contracts and other agreements, nor is it authorized to engage in the interpretation of contracts entered into by private parties. Such matters must instead be addressed by private counsel or by a court.

Requester: Chief Elder Ean Lee Bordeaux. Question: Is the custodian's decision to release the requested records with redactions consistent with the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)? Brief Response: This request poses several specific questions that extend beyond asking whether the custodian's decision regarding employee-related records is consistent with the FOIA. I cannot address those questions because they fall outside the limited authority granted to this Office under A.C.A. § 25-19-105(c)(3)(B)(i). Further, several categories of records identified in the request likely do not constitute personnel or evaluation records. Therefore, any custodial decisions concerning those records likewise fall outside the scope of my review. The only decision that appears to fall within my statutory authority to review is the city's determination that certain records in the "Training Division file" are not subject to disclosure under A.C.A. §§ 25-19-105(b)(12), -105(b)(13), and -105(c)(1). Although I have not reviewed the records at issue, employment applications, background investigations, and personal history statements are ordinarily best classified as personnel records under the FOIA. As such, they are generally subject to disclosure unless the release of particular information would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy or another exemption applies. Accordingly, personnel records ordinarily should not be withheld in their entirety merely because they contain exempt information. Rather, the custodian should redact exempt information and disclose the remainder of the record. Because I have not reviewed the records, however, I cannot say whether any specific record has been properly classified or redacted. Instead, I have set out the legal standards governing the disclosure of personnel records and employee-evaluation records under the FOIA.

Requester: State Senator Missy Irvin. Question 1: Is there any authority in Arkansas law for a county assessor to reappraise property that was assessed as of January 1, 2026 after July 1, 2026 to change the school district on applicable property to a newly isolated school district under Act 919 of 2025? The newly isolated school district was approved by voters at the March 2026 election and became a functioning school district as of July 1, 2026. Question 2: Is there any authority in Arkansas law for a quorum court to levy a millage in its November or December 2026 levy ordinance for a newly isolated school district that became a functioning school district on July 1, 2026 but has not passed a millage approved by voters? Question 3: Is there any authority in Arkansas law for a county treasurer to distribute property tax funds to a school district that has not had a millage levied by quorum court ordinance? Question 4: Under existing Arkansas law, where the subject property was assessed as of January 1, 2026 in the previously consolidated school district, and if the answer to Question 1 is no, is there any way to get the newly isolated school district on the tax statements that go out beginning in February 2027? Question 5: If the county treasurer distributes all of the property tax funds that were assessed and collected for the previously consolidated school district to the previously consolidated school district, should the previously consolidated school district send the appropriate amount of funds to the newly isolated school district? Brief Response: I must respectfully decline to opine on your questions because they are the subject of pending litigation. It is the long-standing policy of the Office of the Attorney General, as a member of the executive branch, to decline to opine on matters that are pending before the courts for resolution.

Requester: State Representative David Ray. Question 1: Under the applicable state and federal law, what authority does a county with no zoning ordinances in place have to regulate a proposed data center before a county construction permit is issued? Brief Response: Under Arkansas law, a county that has not adopted zoning ordinances has limited authority to regulate a proposed data center before issuing a construction permit. It may not deny the permit on zoning or land-use compatibility grounds because no zoning scheme exists under which the proposed use can be prohibited or conditioned. But the county may enforce otherwise valid ordinances and statutory requirements concerning matters such as health and safety, flood-prone areas, subdivision development, road access, setbacks, and applicable building requirements. Question 2: Under the applicable state and federal law, what authority does a county with no zoning ordinances in place have to regulate a data center after a county permit is issued and construction has begun? Question 3: After a county with no zoning ordinances in place has issued a construction permit and construction has begun, does said county have the authority to enact an ordinance changing the requirements for the permit by imposing additional requirements for the permit, increasing the standards to be met or fees to be paid, delaying construction, changing the methods of construction, requiring reports, or increasing compliance expenses? Brief Response: In response to Questions 2 and 3, a county retains regulatory authority after issuing a construction permit; however, in one case the Arkansas Supreme Court held substantial reliance on a building permit equitably estopped the county from revoking the building permit. A permit, standing alone, does not create a contract or a vested right to remain governed by the laws in effect when the permit issued. Thus, the permit holder generally remains subject to later regulations lawfully enacted under the government's police power. Question 4: Under the applicable state and federal law, does a county with no zoning ordinances in place have the authority to enact an ordinance to regulate a data center based upon the amount of electricity or the amount of water it is expected to use, after the data center has secured contracts for such services and the Public Service Commission and the particular utility entities have approved such contracts? Brief Response: Public Service Commission ("PSC") approval of utility-service contracts does not foreclose otherwise lawful county regulation, but the county may not override matters committed to the PSC by the General Assembly. Question 5: If a county with no zoning ordinances in place causes foreseeable damage to a data center through an action that is later determined to be ultra vires on the part of the county, may the county be held liable for such damages in state or federal court? Brief Response: Arkansas Code § 21-9-301 generally immunizes counties from tort liability, including negligence claims, except to the extent the county has applicable liability-insurance coverage. A finding that county action was ultra vires does not itself create a damages remedy or overcome statutory immunity. Rather, ultra vires claims are limited to prospective injunctive relief, and monetary damages may be recovered only if immunity has been waived through applicable insurance coverage. Question 6: After a county issues a construction permit upon the applicant's satisfaction of all conditions, and the applicant enters into contracts on the strength of that permit and begins construction, does said county have the authority to enact an ordinance that retroactively adds conditions to the permit and causes work to cease until new conditions are met? Brief Response: When a permit has been lawfully issued, the permit holder has entered contracts and incurred liabilities in reliance on it, and construction has begun, the Arkansas Supreme Court has held that the permit holder may acquire "a kind of property right" entitled to protection in some circumstances. In _Tankersley Bros. Industries, Inc. v. City of Fayetteville_, the Arkansas Supreme Court explained that, after such reliance, a permit generally may not be revoked without cause or in the absence of public necessity. An ordinance that retroactively adds new permit conditions and stops construction until those conditions are satisfied could therefore operate as a material alteration or effective revocation of the permit and might be subject to challenge under _Tankersley_.

Requester: Mr. Travis Harp. Question: Is the custodian's decision to release the requested records with redactions consistent with the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)? Brief Response: Because I have not been provided with copies of the records at issue, I cannot review the records or determine whether they have been properly classified under the FOIA. Similarly, I cannot determine whether the custodian has properly redacted exempt information. Thus, I cannot definitively state whether the custodian's decision regarding the release of the records is consistent with the FOIA. Instead, I have set out the legal standards governing the disclosure of personnel records and employee-evaluation records under the FOIA.

Requester: Mr. Harry Colman Baker. Question: Is the custodian's decision to withhold records concerning a firefighter's termination as "personnel records" consistent with the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)? Brief Response: It appears that the custodian has determined that the requested records are all personnel records that should be withheld under A.C.A. § 25-19-105(b)(12) because their release would "constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy." Because I have not been provided with the records in question, I cannot determine whether the custodian properly classified the records or whether his decision to withhold them is consistent with the FOIA. But it is unlikely that all of the requested records—"disciplinary records and write-ups, complaints and incident reports, and personnel action forms"—constitute personnel records. I set forth in the opinion the legal standards that the custodian must apply to determine whether to release or withhold the records in question.

Requester: State Representative Dwight Tosh. Question: Does a county possess the legal authority to have and place a county-wide sales tax on the ballot that is solely and entirely dedicated and designated for fire departments within the county? Brief Response: A county's authority to place a county-wide sales tax on the ballot that is solely and entirely dedicated to fire departments within the county depends on the statutory authority under which the tax is levied. Under A.C.A. § 26-73-113, a county may place such a tax on the ballot if the proposed tax's use falls within the permissible uses listed in A.C.A. § 26-73-113(a)(2). Alternatively, under A.C.A. §§ 26-74-201 through -223 or A.C.A. §§ 26-74-301 through -321, a county may place such a tax on the ballot if the ballot title and levying ordinance specify the desired distribution and the affected local governments execute an interlocal agreement concerning that distribution.

Requester: State Senator Missy Irvin. Question 1: In light of the circumstances described in the opinion request, when is the earliest possible time for the county assessor to split the real estate and personal property assessments between the three resulting school districts in Stone County? There has been some suggestion that the assessed values cannot be split out until January 2027. But as explained with the request, this timeline is at odds with the requirement that the millage issue be included on the March 2027 ballot, as the accurate calculation of millage depends on obtaining assessed values before the mid-December ballot submission deadline. Brief Response: Although 2027 is the first assessment year in which Mountain View, Timbo, and Rural Special will exist as separate school districts throughout the entire assessment cycle, nothing in Act 919 of 2025 or the general assessment statutes requires the county assessor to wait until January 2027 to allocate existing assessments among the three districts for purposes of calculating millage rates and preparing for the March 2027 election. Question 2: When is the proper time for the Public Service Commission to split the utility assessment between the three school districts in Stone County and submit this information to the county assessor? Brief Response: The Tax Division's first formal assessment and certification recognizing Mountain View, Timbo, and Rural Special as separate school districts should occur during the 2027 assessment cycle. Act 919 of 2025 does not prescribe a different timeline. Question 3: Detachment of Rural Special and Timbo from the Mountain View School District was completed on July 1, 2026, triggering a direct flow of state funding, including foundation funding, to the Rural Special School District and Timbo School District, respectively. But the local tax payments collected from taxpayers residing in all three school districts in Stone County are being distributed by the county treasurer solely to the Mountain View School District. Is this a proper distribution of the local tax revenue, or should revenue be apportioned across each of the three school districts based upon the school district that currently corresponds with each taxpayer's residence? Question 4: How does the requirement under Article 14, section 3(c)(3) of the Arkansas Constitution apply to the creation of new isolated school districts? Does the revenue derived from a tax levied for the benefit of the taxpayer follow the taxpayer and his or her corresponding real, personal, and utility property as district lines shift beneath them? Question 5: Finally, if the Stone County Treasurer is properly distributing local taxes, then when is the earliest date that the Rural Special and Timbo School Districts must begin receiving local taxes remitted by taxpayers within their respective districts? May Stone County discretionarily distribute tax revenue to the new school districts prior to the date that revenues must be distributed? Brief Response: To answer Questions 3, 4, and 5 together, while the same millage rate continues to be levied on property within the detached districts until a new millage rate is approved, the revenues generated from that property must be directed to the detached district in which the property is located. Once Rural Special School District and Timbo School District became operative on July 1, 2026, local tax revenues remitted by taxpayers residing within their district boundaries should have been apportioned to those districts. If tax revenues attributable to the detached districts have been distributed elsewhere, Arkansas law recognizes certain remedies, although recovery may depend on whether the funds have already been expended.

Requester: Ms. Laura Holzhauer. Question: Is the custodian's decision to release the requested records with redactions consistent with the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)? Brief Response: In my opinion, the custodian's decision to release the records as redacted is consistent with the FOIA. The records at issue are properly classified as personnel records, and the custodian has correctly determined that they are subject to release with redactions.
